content: How can pastors help their churches become more evangelistic without relying on another program? Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss what it takes to build a culture where sharing the gospel becomes a normal part of church life. title: Train Women to Teach the Bible: A 4-Week Plan
summary: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. But where do we find teachers?
summary_zh: 圣经研究是许多教会中妇女部的心跳。 越来越多的教会更喜欢现场教学, 这可能会给妇女部主任带来挑战: 我们在哪里找到老师? 圣经老师不会随时来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。
title_zh: 培训女性教导圣经： 4周计划
content: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. More and more churches have come to prefer live teaching over video studies . But this can present a challenge for women’s ministry directors: Where do we find teachers? Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. Whether women have never taught the Scriptures before or are building on previous experience, we can help them grow and gain confidence in “rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Tim. 2:15) through careful instruction and practice. To equip women in my church to teach, I helped develop a four-session course. Here’s how we developed and implemented this training. Get Organized I first recruited two women with experience teaching the Bible, and together we prepared ourselves as instructors by taking the online Simeon Trust First Principles for Women course. We then personalized the principles we learned to fit our training goals for other women in our church. Since there are different strategies for approaching various genres of Scripture, the first time we held this course, we chose to train women on how to teach an epistle. We selected 1 Peter as our text and assigned each group a passage to work on throughout the course. For example, Group 1 had 1 Peter 1:1–12, Group 2 had 1:13–21, and Group 3 had 4:12–19. We used 5:1–11 as a common passage that we studied as a whole group. In subsequent courses, we chose other genres of Scripture: narrative using passages from a Gospel and wisdom/poetry using a psalm. Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. We promoted the training with a clear purpose: to help participants grow in their ability to understand and teach God’s Word. We spelled out our expectations: attending all four sessions, completing homework, and teaching a 10-minute message to peers. Individual attention in training is key, so we assigned each participant to a small group of three to six women with a leader. The leader gave feedback on homework and answered questions. Teach the Course Here’s what we covered each week, including teaching content, small-group work, and homework assignments. Week 1: Foundations of Study After sharing two foundational truths about the Bible—Scripture is God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16–17) and Scripture is alive and active, changing us as we study it (Heb. 4:12)—we taught three principles. First, we never add to or subtract from what’s written in the Word (Deut. 4:2; 1 Cor. 4:6; Rev. 22:18–19). A Bible text isn’t a jumping-off point to give our insights. We must be diligent to stay faithful to the Holy Spirit’s intended meaning. We strive to “stay on the line” of Scripture , never going above it by adding to it (which can result in undue speculation or legalism) or going below it by taking away from it (avoiding unpleasant or confusing passages, or altering the meaning to what we want it to mean). Second, the Bible is one big story, with one Hero of the story (Luke 24:27). From Genesis to Revelation—creation, fall, redemption, and restoration—we see God at work to reconcile people to himself. The Old Testament points to our need for and anticipation of a Savior, and the New Testament records and reflects on that Savior. Understanding this one big story helps reveal the significance of each passage. Third, context is king and questions are key . Context is the setting in which something occurs, and it always guides our interpretation. We consider both the literary context (what comes before and after a passage) and the historical context (the situation in which the original audience found themselves). To “stay on the line,” asking in-depth questions of the passage is vital, so we introduced the participants to questions for an epistle . In small-group time, we had each woman read the group’s assigned passage aloud because a thoughtful reading aids understanding, as does hearing the passage multiple times. For homework, we asked the women to list 15 observations from their small group’s passage along with 15 observations from the common passage. Week 2: From Text to Talk We started in small groups with each woman sharing her observations on her group’s designated passage. Then we had a whole-group discussion of observations found in the common passage. This week’s teaching focused on how to go from observing a Scripture text to preparing to teach it to a group of real women. We first explained exegesis—analyzing Scripture to draw out its intended meaning. We walked the women through how to use the questions for an epistle to understand the passage’s meaning to the original recipients. We always look for the main idea, the immediate context (passages before and after in the book), the historical context (names, places, situations, other passages that may explain this one), and the biblical context (Where does this fit in the bigger story of the whole Bible?). A concordance is a valuable tool here. We then helped participants find the connection to the gospel (Luke 24:25–27). We taught them to look for related themes (e.g., hope, forgiveness, sacrifice, priesthood) and typology (people, objects, or events patterned after Jesus like Joseph, Boaz, David, or the ark). The Jesus Storybook Bible can be a great help in revealing these connections. Finally, we taught the women how to draw out applications. The main idea doesn’t change because of the audience, but the particular applications may. We emphasized knowing your audience by thinking through where the listeners are spiritually, what sin issues or struggles they have, and what encouragement they need. We reminded the group of the purpose of our messages: to have women’s affections stirred by the Spirit so they’re personally affected by the truth of the text. For homework, each woman identified an audience for her teaching specifying age, life stage, and specific needs and struggles. Then, using her assigned passage, she recorded the main idea, the significance to the original hearers, the connection to the gospel, and an application specific to her target audience. Week 3: Structure and Illustrations In small groups, women shared their homework and instructors gave feedback. While it’s time-consuming for each woman to share, everyone benefits from hearing each other’s work on the same passage. We began this week’s teaching by explaining two common mistakes teachers make: (1) sharing what “touched us” in a passage, unrelated to the main idea, and (2) having so many points that they obstruct the main idea. To avoid these mistakes, we discussed the importance of structure. The process of finding a text’s structure varies depending on its genre, so we briefly explained how to go about determining the “shape” of three genres: epistle, narrative, and poetry. Since we were learning to teach an epistle, we spent the most time on this, helping the women focus on the words and grammar. We taught them to look for “bookends” (similar words at the beginning and end of a paragraph or book); repeated words, phrases, or ideas; connecting words like if/then, because, therefore; grammar and verb tenses; and words that reveal the context. All these help uncover the author’s main idea or emphasis in a discourse. We then took time to practice identifying these elements in small groups using the common passage. A Bible text isn’t a jumping-off point to give our insights. To close week 3, we introduced illustrations. We explained their purpose (to serve the main idea and application and make the teaching clearer) along with various illustration types and where to find them. We suggested using stories, analogies, word pictures, and examples from personal experiences, books, movies, history, current events, and nature. For homework, we asked the women to develop a teaching outline and an illustration for their passage. Week 4: Preparing a Talk The final week began in small groups with each member sharing her teaching outline and illustratio
content_zh:
圣经研究是许多教会中妇女部的心跳。 越来越多的教会更喜欢现场教学, 这可能会给妇女部主任带来挑战: 我们在哪里找到老师? 圣经老师不会随时来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。
无论妇女以前或现在都从未教授过《圣经》,我们都可以通过认真的教学和实践,帮助她们成长并树立“正确处理真理之言”的信心(2 Tim2:15)。 为了让教会里的女人能够教书,我帮助开发了四门课程。 以下是我们如何制定并实施这一培训。
Get Organization I首先招募了两位具有教授圣经经验的女性,我们一起通过在线西门信托基金妇女第一原则课程,准备成为教员。 然后,我们将我们学到的原则个性化,以适应我们为教会中其他妇女的培训目标。
由于有不同的策略 接近各种流派的圣经, 我们第一次举办这个课程, 我们选择培训妇女 如何教授一个故事。 我们挑选了一名彼得作为我们的案文,并指派每个小组在全程中工作一段。 例如,第1组拥有1 Peter 1:1–12,第2组拥有1:13–21,第3组拥有4:12–19.
我们用5:1–11作为我们作为一个整体研究的共同段落. 在随后的课程中,我们选择了其他的经典流派:使用福音书的段落进行叙事,使用诗歌的智慧/诗歌. 圣经老师不会随时来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。
我们以明确的目的促进了培训:帮助参与者提高理解和教授上帝之言的能力。 我们阐述了我们的期望:参加所有四场会议,完成作业,向同行传授十分钟的信息。 对培训的个别关注是关键所在,因此,我们指派每个参与者到一个由3至6名妇女组成的小组,并有一名领导人。
领导对功课进行反馈,回答问题. 包括教学内容、小组工作、家庭作业等。 第1周:研究基础 在分享了两个关于圣经的基本真理之后——书稿是上帝创造的(2 Tim. 3:16-17),圣经是活生生的,在我们研究圣经(Heb.
4:12)——我们教了三项原则. 首先,我们从不增减《言语》中的内容(德国4:2;1 Cor.4:6;Rev.22:18-19)。 圣经的文本不是给我们深刻见解的跳跃点。 我们必须坚持忠于圣灵的本意。
我们努力“坚持”《圣经》,从不增加(这可能导致不适当的猜测或法律主义),或从《圣经》中取下(避免令人不快或令人困惑的段落,或改变我们想要它的含义),从而超越《圣经》。 第二,圣经是一个大故事,有一个故事的英雄(公爵24:27).
从创世纪到启示——创造、堕落、赎罪和恢复——我们看见上帝在努力使人与自己和解。 《旧约》指出了我们对救世主的需求和期待,《新约》记录并反思了该救世主。 了解这个大故事有助于揭示每个段落的意义. 第三,背景是国王,问题是关键。
环境是事物发生的环境,它总是指导我们的解释。 我们既考虑文学背景(一段前后发生的事情),也考虑历史背景(原始观众发现自己的情况). 因此,我们向与会者介绍了一些问题。
我们让每位女性大声读到他们指定的段落, 关于家庭作业,我们要求妇女从其小团体的行经中列出15项意见以及共同行经中的15项意见。
第2周:从文字到谈话 我们开始分成几个小组,每个妇女都分享她对小组指定通道的看法。 然后,我们进行了关于共同段落中发现的意见的全体讨论。 本周的教学重点是如何从观察一本圣经到准备教授给一群真正的妇女。
我们首先解释了解释——分析《圣经》,以找出其意旨。 我们用这些问题来理解这些段落对原始接受者的意义。
我们总是寻找主要思想,即时背景(书中前后的通道),历史背景(名称,地点,情况,其他段落可能解释这一段),以及圣经背景(这与整个圣经中更大的故事在哪里相适应?). 在这里,协调是一个宝贵的工具。 然后,我们帮助参与者找到与福音书的联系(公爵24:25-27)。
我们教他们寻找相关的主题(如希望,宽恕,祭祀,祭祀)和类型(人,物,或以耶稣为图案的事件如约瑟夫,波阿兹,大卫,或方舟). 耶稣故事书圣经可以极大地帮助揭示这些联系. 最后,我们教妇女如何绘制申请表。
主要想法不会因为观众而改变, 我们强调通过思考听众的精神所在、他们的罪恶问题或斗争以及他们需要什么鼓励来了解听众。
我们提醒这群人我们的信息的目的:让心灵激起女性的感情, 对于家庭作业,每个妇女都指定了一个听众来指导她的教学,具体说明年龄、生活阶段以及具体的需要和斗争。
随后,她利用她指定的段落,录制了主要想法,对原听觉者的意义,与福音的连接,以及针对她目标受众的应用程序. 第3周:结构和说明 在小组中,妇女分享她们的家庭作业,教员提供反馈。
虽然每个妇女分享是耗时的,但每个人都能听到对方在同一段的作品。 我们开始本周的教学时, 解释了两个常见的错误:(1) 分享“触摸”我们的东西,
为了避免这些错误,我们讨论了结构的重要性。 寻找文本结构的过程依其流派不同而不同,所以我们简要地解释了如何决定三种流派的“形状 ” : 论语、叙事和诗歌。 自从我们学会教一个学说以来,我们花了最多的时间来研究这个问题,帮助女性专注于文字和语法.
我们教他们寻找“书尾”(一段或书开头和结尾的类似词);重复的词、短语或想法;将词语连接起来,例如如果/当时,因为这样;语法和动词紧张;以及揭示上下文的词语。 所有这些有助于在讨论中揭示作者的主要思想或重点。
然后,我们花了时间,用共同通道将这些因素分成小组。 圣经的文本不是给我们深刻见解的跳跃点。 在第三个星期结束时,我们介绍了插图。 我们解释了它们的目的(服务于主要思想和应用,使教学更加清晰)以及各种插图类型和在哪里找到它们。
我们建议使用故事,类比,文字图片,以及个人经历,书籍,电影,历史,时事和自然中的例子. 关于家庭作业,我们请这些妇女制定教学大纲和说明,供她们通过。 第4周:准备谈话 最后一周开始分成小组,每个成员分享她的教学大纲和插图
author: Nora Allison

title: When Morningness Is Confused with Godliness
summary: Could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical?
summary_zh: 你们应当在早晨和真主在一起享受。 你们应当在白昼中为真主创造最初的时辰。 你们为天经和拜功而早起吧! 它为你们的其余的日子定下调子。
title_zh: 当早晨与虔诚混淆时
content: “Do your quiet time with God every morning.” “Give God your first hours (your best hours!) of the day.” “Rise early for Scripture and prayer; it sets the tone for the rest of your day!” From pulpits to podcasts, I’ve heard these sentiments often in Christian circles. The instructions aren’t just to spend alone time with God but to specifically do so as the very first act of your day. For many, the “morning quiet time” has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. Actor Mark Wahlberg once went viral on Instagram for a screenshot of his morning routine : waking up at 2:30 a.m., praying at 2:45, and completing his first workout before 5:30. This is one of many examples of how early rising has become associated with aspirational godliness. But is it really more virtuous to be a morning person than a night owl? What If You Have to Sleep In? Behind the modern mindset of hyperidealized mornings is the assumption that being a “morning person” is a virtue in and of itself—a gritty choice toward wellness and productivity within everyone’s power. The implication is that if you’re disciplined and wise, you’ll set the alarm clock and start the day early; you’ll make it happen. If you’re slothful or foolish, you won’t. Extenuating circumstances are just excuses. For many, the ‘morning quiet time’ has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. But what would this mean for nurses whose work begins and ends when it’s dark outside? What about parents with newborns, whose babies’ demands don’t abide by our ideal rhythms? How about Christians who are naturally night owls: most alert, focused, and productive at night? Should these folks just suck it up and aspire to get up earlier in spite of their circumstances? Or could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical? God Loves Early Risers At first glance, it might seem that God’s Word does value our mornings most. Pastor David Mathis wrote an insightful article summarizing the abundance of instances in Scripture in which God’s people (including Christ himself!) either rose early to good effect or were directed by God to do so. Consider the Psalms: In Psalm 5:3, David says, “O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice.” In Psalm 88:13, the Sons of Korah sing, “In the morning my prayer comes before you.” In Psalm 90:14, Moses prays to God, “Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.” God clearly meets with his people in the morning. Case closed? Not quite. When you consult the whole counsel of Scripture, it becomes clear that God emphasizes meditating on his Word, singing his praises, and praying to his name just as much in the night as in the morning. Nocturnal Worship Let’s explore some nighttime examples. In Acts 16:25–26, after Paul and Silas are imprisoned in Philippi, God’s Word notably mentions the timing of their worship: “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God . . .” Silas and Paul don’t try to go to sleep early so they can engage with God at the crack of dawn. They stay up late, worshiping at midnight. The results are profound. In Psalm 63:5–6, David prays to the Lord, “My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips, when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night.” This psalm as a whole is arguably a nighttime prayer. David prays these lyrics to the Lord seemingly all while on his “bed,” singing midnight praises. Consider Jesus’s earthly life. On the fateful day before his crucifixion, when it comes to spending devoted time alone with his Father, Jesus prays passionately, in Gethsemane, at night (Matt. 26:36–56). There is no mention in the Gospels of Jesus rising early on this momentous day; it might have happened, but the recorded emphasis is Jesus’s spiritual devotion in the dark. Morning and evening aren’t pitted against each other in the Bible. They’re a complementary pair: Psalm 77:2 says, “In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying.” Psalm 88:1 says, “O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you.” Psalm 92:1–2 says, “It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night.” What does this mean for practical living? If you’ve never tried it, consider adding nighttime worship to your spiritual toolbox. Carve out time to pray, praise, and ponder the Scriptures before bed. If you struggle with insomnia, see it as a devotional opportunity. If your brain just won’t turn off at 3:00 a.m., fellowship with your Maker rather than letting your mind wander aimlessly. In a unique season of spiritual desperation, set your alarm clock for the middle of the night, to wait on the Lord under the stars, to intently watch for his presence and answers to prayer (Ps. 130:6). Dreams can be God’s chosen instrument to instruct and encourage his people (e.g., Gen. 28:10–22; 37:6–7; 1 Kings 3:5; Matt. 1:20–21; 2:13; Acts 2:17). Dreams appear in Scripture as a meaningful spiritual realm, and the thoughts you think in the final moments before sleep often seep into your nightly imagination. What better way to end your day than to fill your mind with God and his excellencies, to draw your heart near to his love, and to pray for spiritual protection while you slumber. Ultimately, if mornings are a perpetual struggle for you, release yourself from the guilt and legalism of needing to give God a half hour every morning. Give him your nights! Balanced Worship If you’ve found it fruitful to rise early to devote alone time to God, continue doing so with discipline and joy. But beware of imposing your own daily spiritual practices on others with a prideful narrow-mindedness that Scripture lacks. Release yourself from the guilt and legalism of needing to give God a half hour every morning. Give him your nights! Excessive sleeping can be a sign of sinful sloth (Prov. 19:15). But biblically, the godly Christian can please God just as much staying up late to worship as rising early. Both routes are biblical and blessed. The mature Christian life, across different seasons, will have various rhythms of dedicated worship at all times of the day and night: sometimes at the crack of dawn, other times at noon, or even in the dark (Deut. 6:4–7). Sacrifice your mornings to the Lord when you’re able. Devote your evenings too.
content_zh:
你们应当在早晨和真主在一起享受。 你们应当在白昼中为真主创造最初的时辰。 你们为天经和拜功而早起吧!它为你们的其余的日子定下调子。 我经常在基督教圈子里听到这些情绪, 这些指示不仅仅是与上帝单独相处,
对许多人来说,“早晨的宁静时间”已经成为衡量你与上帝关系如何的尺度。 演员Mark Wahlberg曾经在Instagram上进行病毒传播, 这是许多例子之一,说明早起如何与渴望的虔诚联系在一起。
但做个早起的人 比做个夜猫子好吗? 如果你必须睡觉呢? 现代思想认为, " 晨光人 " 本身就是一种美德 -- -- 在每个人的权力范围内对健康和生产力的粗暴选择。
也就是说,如果你有纪律和智慧,你会设置警报钟,并提前开工;你会让它实现。 如果你懒惰或愚蠢, 减轻罪责只是借口 对许多人来说,`早晨的平静时间'已成为衡量你与上帝关系如何的尺度。
这对护士来说意味着什么? 父母若有新生儿, 基督教徒自然是夜猫子, 这些人是否应该吸起来 渴望早起 不顾自己的处境?
或者说,我们理想化的清晨宁静时期,是否比圣经更具有文化色彩? 上帝爱早起者 乍一看,上帝的言语似乎对我们的早晨最为重要。
大卫·马西斯牧师写了一篇深刻的文章,总结了圣经中大量的例子,其中上帝的百姓(包括基督本人)不是早起,就是奉上帝的指示这样做。
你看看《古兰经》。在《古兰经》5:3中,大卫说:耶和华啊!你在早晨听见我的声音。 在"诗经"第88卷第13节中,可拉之子们唱道:"早晨,我的祈祷降临你们面前。 在《诗经》第90章第14节中,穆萨祈祷真主说:你们以你们的坚忍的爱,在早晨拯救我们,以便我们快乐和快乐。 早晨,上帝显然与他的族人相会。 结案? 没有
当你参考整个天经的教诲时,显然上帝强调冥想他的言语,歌颂他的赞美,在黑夜和早晨一样祈祷他的名字. 夜礼拜 让我们来探索一些夜间的例子。
在16:25-26号法案中,保罗和西拉斯被囚禁在菲利皮之后,上帝的言语特别提到了他们的崇拜时间:"大约午夜保罗和西拉斯在向上帝祈祷和歌颂. Silas和Paul不会早睡, 他们熬夜,午夜礼拜 其结果是深刻的。
在"诗经"卷63:5-6中,大卫向主祈祷说:"我的灵魂将满足于肥美的食物,我的嘴将喜悦地赞颂你,当我想起你在我的床上,并在黑夜的表里思念你。 这整个诗歌可以说是夜祷. 大卫在他“床上”唱午夜赞美时,
想想耶稣的地球生活。 在他被钉十字架的前一天,在与父亲单独度过时间的时候,耶稣在夜里热切地祈祷在Gethsemane(Matt. 26:36-56). 福音书中没有提到耶稣在这个重要的日子提前升起;它可能已经发生,但记录的强调是耶稣在黑暗中的精神奉献.
早晚并不在圣经中相互对立。 他们是一个互补的对:诗篇77:2说,“在我麻烦的一天里,我寻求主;在夜晚,我的手被伸开而不磨损。” "诗经"第88卷第1节说:"耶和华啊!我的救赎之神啊!我昼夜在你们面前呐喊。 诗篇92: 1–2说: " 向耶和华致谢,赞颂你的名字是件好事,至尊者啊!
在早晨和晚上,你应当说出你坚定的情谊。 这对实际生活意味着什么? 若你从未尝试过, 刻意祈祷、赞美、在睡觉前思索天经。 如果你与失眠作斗争, 把它视为一个奉献的机会。
如果你的大脑不会在凌晨3点关闭, 在一个独特的精神绝望的季节,将你的闹钟定在半夜,在星辰下等待主,有意地看着他的出现和对祈祷的回答(Ps130:6).
梦可以是上帝选择用来指示和鼓励其人民的工具(例如:Gen. 28:10–22;37:6–7;1 Kings 3:5;Matt. 1:20–21;2:13;Act 2:17). 梦境在圣经中作为一个有意义的精神领域出现,在睡眠前的最后时刻你所想的思想常常渗入你的夜梦中.
结束你的一天比用上帝和他卓越的神灵 让你的心接近他的爱 以及趁你睡着时祈祷精神保护更好的方法 归根结底,如果早晨对你来说是永恒的挣扎,那么就从每天早上需要给上帝一个半小时的内疚和法律主义中解放出来. 给他你的夜晚!
平衡礼拜 如果你发现早起为上帝奉献时间, 但当心将自己的日常精神实践 强加于别人 以骄傲的狭隘的思想, 而圣经缺乏。 让自己摆脱每天早上需要给上帝半小时的内疚和法律主义. 给他你的夜晚!
过度睡眠可能代表罪恶的懒惰(19:15,普罗夫)。 但圣经上,虔诚的基督教徒可以取悦上帝 就像早起一样 晚起崇拜 这两条路线都是圣经性的和吉祥的.
成熟的基督教生活,跨越不同的季节,在白天和夜晚的任何时候都会有各种献身崇拜的节奏:有时在黎明的裂缝,其他时候在中午,甚至黑暗中(德国6:4-7). 尽你所能为主牺牲早晨。 将你的夜晚也。
author: Cole Mizel

title: Contend Without Being Contentious
summary: In an age marked by theological compromise and unnecessary outrage, we need church leaders who can do more than win arguments.
summary_zh: “我们如何在不争吵和争论的情况下,为信仰而争辩呢? ” 我(Barry)的一位教友在研究Jude的信时, Jude在宗旨声明(vv. 3–4)中表示, 然而,他认为有必要敦促他们“继续信仰”。
title_zh: 在不引起争议的情况下进行竞争
content: “How do we contend for the faith biblically without becoming quarrelsome and contentious?” A member of my (Barry’s) congregation posed this thoughtful yet difficult question when our church was studying the letter of Jude. In his purpose statement (vv. 3–4), Jude says he wants to write about the salvation he shares in common with his recipients. However, he finds it necessary instead to exhort them to “contend for the faith.” What does obeying this exhortation involve? Before we contend for the faith, it’s essential to clarify how to approach confrontation and why we’re seeking to confront in the first place. Knowing myself, I (Ben) can have many sinful and unhelpful reasons for confronting; my pride often tempts me to seek my glory in confrontation rather than seeking the Lord’s glory. Yet when our motivation is wrong, our manner is too. Then, contending can quickly become contentiousness. Jude gives us a better way. Why and How To Confront His letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. Jude provides four basic confrontation categories that will help us defend the truth without becoming quarrelsome. 1. Oppose deceivers (v. 4). We must be able to distinguish between those who are confused and those who are deceivers. Not everyone who errs is a malicious false teacher. Some simply need patient guidance, instruction, and compassionate discipleship. Jude’s letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. But others actively promote error, refuse to submit to biblical authority, or sow seeds of division that can lead God’s people away from Christ. Jude has deceivers in mind as his primary concern in his letter. He’s concerned not just that they’re in error but that they’re influential. For that reason, he wants the church to have the Spirit-led courage to confront the deceivers’ errors. Such contending requires wisdom. For pastors, it can involve correcting false teaching both privately and publicly. You may need to warn your church about dangerous influences or refuse to give a platform to those who persistently distort the gospel. Remember, Paul instructs elders to rebuke those who contradict sound doctrine (Titus 1:9) and to protect God’s flock from spiritual wolves (Acts 20:28–31). He also warns congregations to watch out for divisive teachers (Rom. 16:17–18). When we confront deceivers, our aim isn’t to embarrass them or to win arguments. Rather, we contend for the faith because truth matters and because Christ’s church matters. 2. Instruct doubters (v. 22). In the Christian life, we encounter many who have doubts about the faith. They know the truth, but they struggle to believe it. Instructing those who doubt may not seem like contending for the faith at first, but gently clearing up their concerns strengthens both their faith and the church’s faith. Contending well for doubters can prevent them from wandering or even from becoming deceivers. It’s an act of mercy (v. 22), and it must be done mercifully. When believers doubt or begin to waver on the truth, our responsibility isn’t to ruthlessly force truth on them. We also shouldn’t ignore their questions. Neither response is merciful. Instead, we must engage doubters’ questions with compassion, trusting that the Lord will reveal truth to them in his time. Our belief in Scripture’s sufficiency is critical here. God’s Word, not our teaching or apologetic skill, possesses the power to reveal his truth. Doubts are many and various, but the Bible remains constant and trustworthy. 3. Warn wanderers (v. 23). Between doubting and deceiving stands another category: wandering. Some in the church drift, or have drifted, toward dangerous doctrinal error or patterns of sin that, if left unchecked, will lead to their fall. Jude prescribes the appropriate response: “Save others by snatching them out of the fire” (v. 23). His imagery conveys urgency. Those who wander are on the verge of spiritual catastrophe, so drastic measures are necessary. Many Christians hesitate to confront because warning a fellow church member can feel uncomfortable and intrusive. But God’s Word regularly warns. It does so sternly but as an act of love. For example, Jesus instructs believers to pursue a sinning brother so he might repent and be restored (Matt. 18:15–17). Paul tells the Galatians to restore those caught in transgression with a spirit of gentleness (6:1). And James writes that bringing back a wandering sinner saves him from destruction (5:19–20). When we confront a wanderer, the goal is never condemnation but rescue. Jude calls us to urgent action because drift is spiritually dangerous. We’re to speak the truth in love so that members of Christ’s body, from the least to the greatest, may grow in every respect to maturity under his headship (Eph. 4:15). 4. Guard your heart (vv. 20–21). In all our contending, Jude tells us to guard our hearts. This is unique among Jude’s contention categories because it’s the only one with an inward focus. When we contend, we’re on the offense, fighting for others’ souls. But we must also play defense, guarding the ground God has already claimed in our own hearts. God’s Word, not our teaching or apologetic skill, possesses the power to reveal his truth. How do we guard our hearts? How do we keep ourselves in the love of God (v. 21)? Jude offers three ways: build up your faith, pray, and wait expectantly for the Lord Jesus’s mercy (vv. 20–21). The first two seem obvious. Of course building your faith through God’s Word and prayer will keep you from being deceived. However, Jude’s third instruction requires more thought. Waiting seems passive, but it’s an expectant act of faith that involves grounding our hearts in the gospel—actively remembering that Jesus is the One who is able to keep us from stumbling and who will finally make us stand in his glorious presence (vv. 24–25). Before You Contend We guard our hearts because running into confrontation too hastily only results in contentiousness. This quality is unbefitting of Christians, and particularly of church leaders (1 Tim. 3:3; 2 Tim. 2:22–26). So be adequately prepared before you step in. Clarify your approach so you bring the right motivation and tone to each situation. Guard your heart, and above all, pray for yourself, your church, and those with whom you’re contending. In an age marked by theological compromise and unnecessary outrage, we need church leaders who can do more than win arguments. We need elders, pastors, teachers, and faithful church members who know how to contend wisely, courageously, and graciously.

当面对欺骗者时, 相反,我们为信仰而斗争,因为真理很重要,而基督的教会也很重要。 2. 指示怀疑者(v.22)。 在基督教生活中,我们遇到许多对信仰有疑虑的人. 他们知道真相,但他们很难相信

许多基督徒对峙犹豫不决,因为警告一个教会成员会感到不舒服和侵扰. 但真主的命令是经常警告的。 它如此严厉,但是一种爱的行为。 例如,耶稣指示信徒追逐一个有罪的兄弟,以便他悔改并被恢复(Matt. 18:15-17)。

author: Barry Gibson, Ben Dixon

title: Editor’s Pick: New Children’s Picture Books
summary: Let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment and, even as it changes to something new, that God’s goodness is everlasting.
summary_zh: 秋是变之季. 在我们家里,随着叶子变黄,日子缩短,我最小的孩子开始上中学。 这意味着图片书让我觉得过去有些怀旧, 与很多刺激的事物一起, 来一些新的东西。 许多这些书是关于大变革和适应它们,比如与新婴儿一起生活,搬到新地方,或者在基督的王国中找到新的心脏.
title_zh: 编辑精选：全新儿童图画书
content: Autumn is a season of changes. At our home, as the leaves yellowed and the days shortened, my youngest child started middle school. That means picture books have me feeling a little nostalgia for the past these days, right alongside a lot of excitement for new things to come. Many of these books are about big changes and adjusting to them, like living with a new baby, moving to a new place, or finding a new heart in Christ’s kingdom. But some are also about the little changes happening around us every day, like laughter over a fleeting moment of childhood imagination or settling down to sleep to prepare for a new day. With all these experiences arriving on the horizon and then flying past like interstate billboards, it’s sweet to remember that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). As you hand one of these brand-new books to a young reader or curl up to enjoy it together, let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment, even as it is changing to something new, and that God’s goodness is everlasting. 1. God Gives Sleep by Betsy Childs Howard, illustrated by Bethan Welby ( TGC Store | Amazon) When our family was exhausted and planning a big move with four children ages 6 and under, I really could have used this little book from Betsy Childs Howard. God Gives Sleep is a rhyming board book with illustrations of adorable animals (sleeping ladybugs!) and two simple refrains that even very young listeners can repeat or “read” for themselves: “God gives sleep” and “God will keep.” Both reflect promises from God that feel vital to the early days of parenting filled with sweet, sleepy snuggles and long, sleepless nights. The last picture shows the entire family asleep and includes Isaiah 40:31 (“Those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength,” NIV). God Gives Sleep is engaging, gentle, funny, and wise, and I’ve already given it to parents of new babies. 2. Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel by A. A. Milne, adapted by Kevan Chandler and Joe Sutphin ( Amazon ) Full disclosure: I’m a huge Pooh fan. I’ve probably read the original Milne book dozens of times, and I can be a little sniffy about adaptations. But I loved this one. While I missed Milne’s distinctive narration in parts of the storytelling, this graphic novel retains enough of the original language and has such beautiful artwork that it easily justifies its existence. Parents of young independent readers often ask me for recommendations for books complex enough to be engaging but with content and formatting suitable for early elementary school. This version perfectly fits that space where 6-to-9-year-olds can track the story through the pictures but also enjoy the challenge of some complex vocabulary (“Sudden and Temporary Immersion”) and jokes that reward context research (“An ambush is a sort of Surprise.” “So is a gorse-bush sometimes.”). Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel is a sweet and worthy tribute to this classic celebration of early childhood in all its imaginative wonder. 3. The Upside-Down, Inside-Out, Can’t-Believe-It Kingdom by Jonathan Landry Cruse, illustrated by Joe Hox ( Amazon ) The adventure begins with a son begging his father to tell him an exciting bedtime story with dragons and knights. The result is this retelling of the gospel as a quest with a king and a prince and a reminder of our humble place in the kingdom. Joe Hox’s illustrations stand out for being traditional and bright, with a dragon that isn’t too fierce for younger readers but also enough detail within the pictures to engage older readers. The story tells us that the good King will “make us be strong with the strength of His might,” a powerful message for young knights who want to do great things for the kingdom. 4. Doing Something New: A Prayer for Beginnings by Mitali Perkins, illustrated by Andrés Landazábal ( Amazon ) Mitali Perkins includes a note in the back of Doing Something New about how she moved many times in childhood: “By the time we settled in California for seventh grade, we had lived in India, Ghana, Cameroon, England, Mexico, and New York.” Changes often come with both losses and gains, and Perkins writes with sympathy and encouragement for children walking through all sorts of new experiences. The text reminds readers to live like Jesus—showing love, courage, and kindness—with the knowledge that Jesus also walked through hard experiences and that he’s with us now, wherever we go. The pictures include what appear to be a new school, new friends, new seasons, and the potential loss of or separation from a loved one. The rhyming words offer this prayer to Christ as a resource for others experiencing changes—“You trusted God and God helped you / Here I am, Lord—help me too.” Also check out these books: Jude and the Extraordinary, Spectacular, Miraculous Day: A Creative Retelling of the Feeding of the 5,000 by Jessica Dennis Bush features beautiful mosaic illustrations that look refreshingly like real art rather than AI and a message about offering Jesus what we have. ( TGC Store | Amazon ) Made like Me: A True Story from the Beginning of Everything by Jen Wilkin (with illustrations by Rommel Ruiz) tells the story of the creation of the world with vibrant, kinetic illustrations and an emphasis on how we were designed for community from the beginning of time. ( TGC Store | Amazon ) The Mansoul Chronicles, Book 2: The Schemes and Snares of Diabolus by Tyler Van Halteren (with illustrations by Uyen Nguyen and Aleksander Jasinski) is an illustrated chapter book retelling a John Bunyan story from the 1600s with surprisingly relevant themes for Christians today. ( Amazon ) The Sweetest of Lemons by Daniel Nayeri (with illustrations by Rahele Jomepour Bell) is both a true story and a fairy tale about “a lemon so perfectly sweet it cured sadness itself.” Like the best fairy stories, it carries themes of courage, perseverance, longing, and—most importantly—hope, acknowledging hardship but resting in the certainty of goodness on the horizon. ( Amazon ) Where Wonder Leads: An Adventure in God’s Wild and Wonderful World by Eryn Lynum (with illustrations by Chiara Fedele) is from the host of the Nat Theo podcast and somehow manages to touch on grief, nature activities, profound theology, and fascinating scientific facts in just over 100 illustrated pages. ( Amazon )
content_zh:
秋是变之季. 在我们家里,随着叶子变黄,日子缩短,我最小的孩子开始上中学。 这意味着图片书让我觉得过去有些怀旧, 与很多刺激的事物一起, 来一些新的东西。
许多这些书是关于大变革和适应它们,比如与新婴儿一起生活,搬到新地方,或者在基督的王国中找到新的心脏. 但有些人还谈到我们周围每天发生的一些小变化,比如在童年短暂的想象中欢笑或沉睡,准备新的一天。
在所有这些经历到达地平线后, 然后像州际告示牌一样飞过, 记得“每一个好的礼物和完美的礼物都来自上面,

title: How Memorizing the Sermon on the Mount Reorders My Heart
summary: In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount.
summary_zh: 几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上的塞门(Matt. 5-7)。 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年中, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最著名的布道 用于记忆更具有变革性。 约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道,山上的塞尔蒙人“是[耶穌]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的一件事,因为这是他自己对他希望追随者成为和做的事情的描述。
title_zh: 背诵登山宝训如何重塑我的心
content: A couple of years ago, two college students challenged me—a woman in her 50s—to memorize the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7). Inwardly, I balked, but now I know that few things in my 35 years of following Jesus have been more transformative than committing Jesus’s most famous sermon to memory. John Stott wrote that the Sermon on the Mount is “the nearest thing to a manifesto that [Jesus] ever uttered, for it is his own description of what he wanted his followers to be and to do.” After spending the last few years memorizing it, I see with increasing clarity that I need Jesus’s help to live out what he taught. In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount. Create a New Algorithm The algorithm often knows us better than we know ourselves. Every time we buy something on Amazon or pause to watch a reel on social media, the algorithm chronicles our activities and builds a profile of us. This profile shows our real interests (not just the ones we list in our social media bios) and some of our most private behaviors (the ones we thank God aren’t live streamed). In milliseconds, companies use what the algorithm knows about us to discover the most effective way to get us to buy their products. In the same way that the algorithm learns about us with each post we like and each reel we watch, God’s Word comes alive in us with every command we learn and put into practice, with every verse we ponder, and with every teaching we adopt as a way of life. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Let Scripture Reorder Your Heart Before I started my memorization project, I’d heard many Christians tout Scripture memory as one of the most potent tools for conforming to Jesus, but I didn’t take it seriously. All that changed when I realized algorithms had more access to my life than God’s Word did. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Like many Americans, I was averaging more than two hours daily scrolling social media and shopping online, and much less time reading the Bible. I’d thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. Memorizing and studying the Sermon on the Mount has provided a powerful reset. I’ve noticed two significant changes in my life. 1. My thoughts are increasingly populated by Jesus’s desires for me. Previously, I was easily shaped by what internet influencers said I should be doing and what my heart really wanted to do. Now, Scripture tenderly draws me to Christ’s transforming grace. For example, a few months ago, someone wrote harsh words to me. I couldn’t sidestep what I’d memorized: Pray for those who hurt you (Mt. 5:44) In those difficult interactions, Jesus’s teaching gave me wisdom to stop reacting and start praying for the one lashing out. Pausing to pray breaks down my self-protective stance so I can consider what the log in my eye might be (Mt. 7:5). 2. I see how vastly different God’s kingdom is from the world we live in. I no longer feel as drawn to the shallow version of perfection the algorithm offers me—the beautiful home, the perfectly fit woman charmingly dressed, or the promise of perpetual travel. When I stop to linger over another picture-perfect kitchen, the Sermon on the Mount prompts me to consider where my treasure really is. These chapters have given me a robust lens through which I can view all of God’s Word. After drinking so deeply of Jesus’s sermon , I see it as the hinge on which both the Old Testament and the New Testament hang. I had thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. When Jesus equates murder with anger, he exposes a corruption we prefer not to acknowledge within ourselves (Matt. 5:21–26). Later in the New Testament, we see we have a Savior who forgives our anger and frees us to live to God’s glory. Having this framework embedded in my mind helps me remember the gospel when outside influences pull my attention away. The first three years of my journey into the Sermon on the Mount have helped me be more like Jesus. Yet it’s obvious to me that my journey has just begun. My life changed when those two college students challenged me to memorize the sermon. Almost every day, those words draw me closer to my Savior and encourage me to conform to him. The Sermon on the Mount has given me more joy than any product the algorithm could ever pop into my newsfeed.
content_zh:
几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上的塞门(Matt. 5-7)。 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年中, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最著名的布道 用于记忆更具有变革性。
约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道,山上的塞尔蒙人“是[耶穌]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的一件事,因为这是他自己对他希望追随者成为和做的事情的描述。” 我越来越清楚地看到,我需要耶稣的帮助来维持他所教的。
在一个算法捕捉到我们感情并通过我们的渴望引诱我们上线的世界中,我们能够采用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习和记住圣经——特别是山上的塞门. 创建新算法 算法常常比我们自己更了解我们.
每次我们在亚马逊买东西或暂停观看社交媒体的片段, 算法会记录我们的活动, 这个简介显示了我们的真正兴趣(不只是我们在社交媒体生记中列出的那些),
在毫秒内,公司利用算法了解我们的情况,发现最有效的方法,让我们购买他们的产品. 正如算法用我们喜欢的每一个帖子和我们看的每一卷片子来了解我们一样,上帝的言语以我们学习和运用的每一个命令、我们思考的每一个诗句,以及我们采纳的作为生活方式的每一个教义,在我们的体内充满活力。
通过吸收和服从耶稣在山上的塞尔门,我们可以建立一个反馈循环,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 在开始我的回忆计划之前, 我听到许多基督徒把圣经记忆说成是符合耶稣的最有力工具之一,
当我意识到算法能比上帝的话更能进入我的生活时, 通过吸收和服从耶稣在山上的塞尔门,我们可以建立一个反馈循环,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 我和许多美国人一样,每天平均有两个多小时 滚动社交媒体和网上购物, 阅读圣经的时间要少得多。
我本以为缺乏时间是记忆圣经的最大障碍。 但实际上,我的感情和优先考虑是障碍。 纪念和研究山上的塞蒙号提供了强大的重置. 我注意到我一生中有两个重大的变化。 1. 我的思想日益为耶稣对我的愿望所吸引。
之前,我很容易被网络影响者 说我应该做什么 和我的心真正想要做什么。 现在,圣经轻轻地吸引我走向基督的恩典。 例如,几个月前,有人给我写了严酷的文字. 我无法回避我所记住的:为伤害你的人祈祷(Mt.
5:44。 在这些困难的相互作用中,耶稣的教导给了我智慧,让我停止反应,开始为那一个狂欢祈祷。 暂停祈祷 打破自我保护的姿势 这样我就可以想一想我的眼中的木头是什么(Mt.7:5). 2. 我看到上帝的王国与我们生活的世界大不相同。
我不再觉得算法能给我一个美丽的家, 一个穿得漂亮、体格完美的女人, 当我停止停留 在另一个图片完美的厨房, 山上的赛蒙 促使我考虑 我的宝藏到底在哪里。
这些章节给了我一个强壮的镜头,我可以通过这些镜头观看上帝的所有言语。 在喝完耶稣的布道之后,我认为这是《旧约》和《新约》所依赖的。 我以为没有时间 是我记起圣经的最大障碍 但实际上,我的感情和优先考虑是障碍。
当耶稣将谋杀等同于愤怒时,他揭露了我们不愿承认的腐败(Matt. 5:21-26)。 在后来的"新约"中,我们看到我们有一个救世主,他宽恕了我们的愤怒,让我们自由,活在上帝的荣耀中. 将这个框架嵌入我的脑海, 帮助我记住,当外部影响 吸引我的注意力。
我进入山上的塞尔门旅行的前三年帮助我更像耶稣. 但对我来说, 当两个大学生要求我记住布道时,我的生活就变了。 这些话几乎每天都让我更接近我的救世主,鼓励我服从他.
山上的赛蒙给了我更多的快乐 比任何产品 算法可能涌进我的新闻。
author: Kim Miller

title: Who Is the God of the Bible?
summary: Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope.
summary_zh: 根据贝尔吉克的忏悔书,上帝在两个 " 书 " 中向我们揭示自己:自然之书(真主的世界)和天经之书(真主所写的文字)。 上帝在圣经书中主要揭示自己的方式是宣布他的名字. 在TGC25的两首对联讲座中,斯科特·斯温(Scott Swain)考虑了上帝在圣经中揭示自己的几个名字. 让上帝更深刻地了解他的存在和属性,并为我们的信仰和希望奠定更坚实的基础。
title_zh: 谁是圣经中的神？
content: According to the Belgic Confession , God reveals himself to us in two “books”: the book of nature (God’s world) and the book of Scripture (God’s written Word). The primary way God reveals himself in the book of Scripture is by proclaiming his name. In this first of two paired lectures from TGC25, Scott Swain considers several of the names whereby God reveals himself in the Bible. Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope. It also helps us better appreciate the ways God reveals himself to us in Jesus Christ. title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Finds New Inspiration in an Old Story
summary: ‘I Play Rocky’ is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told.
summary_zh: Rocky在50年前的电影院首映, 1976年, 紧接着是一部布洛克和批判性的亲爱的电影(1976年最令人毛骨悚然的电影和最佳影片奥斯卡奖得主),从此成为美国电影院的一部泛神电影. 洛基在费城的布局和劣势中,对富人的故事抓住了美国令人费解的乐观情绪,这在1970年代中期给了人们必要的灵感,今天仍然有共鸣。 现在在2026年——美国半百周年—— 洛基正在获得戏剧再释放 而一部新电影,I Play Rocky(今天在部分剧场出演)讲述了标志性电影的发展故事,这部电影是它本身的逊色史诗.
title_zh: 《我扮演洛基》在古老的故事中寻找新的灵感
content: Rocky debuted in theaters 50 years ago, in 1976—a bicentennial-year release that underscored the movie’s profound American spirit. Immediately a blockbuster and critical darling (the highest-grossing movie of 1976 and winner of the Best Picture Oscar), it has since become a pantheon film in American cinema. Rocky ’s Philadelphia setting and underdog, rags-to-riches story captured a hardscrabble American optimism, something that gave needed inspiration in the mid-1970s and resonates still today. Now in 2026—America’s semiquincentennial— Rocky is getting a theatrical rerelease. And a new movie, I Play Rocky (out today in select theaters) is telling the story of the iconic movie’s development, which is an underdog epic of its own. The movie, directed by Peter Farrelly ( Green Book ) and starring Anthony Ippolito in a breakout turn as Sylvester Stallone, is a refreshingly feel-good crowd pleaser. It’s the sort of well-made, intelligent, but also inspiring movie for grown-ups that feels like a dying breed in Hollywood. Movies About Moviemaking I Play Rocky (rated PG-13 for language) follows a well-worn template of a movie about the making of a classic movie. Saving Mr. Banks (2013) was about Walt Disney and the making of Mary Poppins . Hitchcock (2012) was about Alfred Hitchcock and the making of Psycho . Last year’s Nouvelle Vague was about Jean-Luc Godard and the making of Breathless . I Play Rocky is about Stallone and the making of Rocky . Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Self-reflexive inspiration goes back more than a century in cinema, perhaps starting with Dziga Vertov’s Man with a Movie Camera (1929). The 1950s produced classics like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Singin’ in the Rain (1952), but the trend really picked up in the postmodern era in the 1960s and beyond: 8 ½ (1963), Day for Night (1973), Mulholland Drive (2001), Adaptation (2002), The Artist (2011), and Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood (2019). The list is long. A hallmark of postmodernity is a metaposture of knowing awareness—storytellers who know they’re storytellers and want the audience to know that they know. As postmodernism has given way to metamodernism , the trend of “movies about moviemaking” has continued, but in a slightly different register. These sorts of films are no longer merely metaexercises in self-awareness. The cerebral, cynical detachment of “films about filmmaking” like Barton Fink (1991), Ed Wood (1994), or even Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) has given way to metamodern expressions that blend cynicism and sincerity, self-awareness with earnest escapism. Steven Spielberg’s The Fabelmans (2022) is a recent example of a movie in this vein, and I Play Rocky has a similar feel. Even as it lifts the veil on the Hollywood myth factory and mines many laughs out of the fundamentally profit-seeking, money-centric nature of the movie business, it’s full of heart and soul. It has a joyful, hopeful, sincere, perhaps idealistic spirit (“I’d rather be an optimist and be wrong, than a pessimist and be right,” one character says). Refreshing Celebration of Marriage I also like how I Play Rocky celebrates the empowering beauty of marriage. The film opens with Stallone as a broke actor in New York, sometimes sleeping on the streets and at one point accepting a role in an X-rated adult film just to earn some desperately needed money (a dark part of Stallone’s past that the film plays for awkward laughs). He’s a lost soul with bleak prospects. But then he meets Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), with whom he works at a movie theater. They get married and move to Los Angeles, and things start to turn around for him. As a husband and soon a father, Stallone feels more urgency to provide. He valets at a swanky Hollywood restaurant to pay the bills while he churns out scripts that he tries to get into influential hands. Sasha types the scripts for him and encourages him at every turn, even as they struggle to pay rent. At one point, she reminds him, “It’s not just you against the world. It’s us against the world.” She’s his ally and cheerleader, believing in him when few else do. Stallone’s parents were divorced, and he had a complicated relationship with his father, Frank (Matt Dillon). Yet I Play Rocky doesn’t play the “blame my parents for all my trauma” card—which is also refreshing. At one point, Stallone says, “My dad, he messed up a lot. But it’s my life.” Stallone doesn’t blame anyone else for the bad choices he’s made or the setbacks he’s had. His story is his own. At a time when it seems every other movie is some version of therapeutic moral absolution for sinners and villains , on account of their broken upbringing, it’s nice to have a movie that pushes back against this. “It’s my story,” Stallone tells the producers who want to turn his Rocky script into a film. “So I play Rocky.” Searching for Stories We used to just tell stories. Now we tell stories about stories. We write books about story and the spiritual deprivation of a destoried world . We hunger for old stories but struggle to invent new ones . Hence the appeal of a movie like I Play Rocky , which finds new narrative inspiration only by mining a classic. Our contemporary world is so uprooted, so unplaced in space and time, so rattled and wearied by what Hartmut Rosa calls “ social acceleration ,” that we feel removed or alienated from our own stories. We’re simultaneously hyperskeptical of the stories we’re told (you see this clearly in the popularity of You Can See Everything ) and deeply hungry to find our own story, to be situated in a compelling narrative that’s going somewhere and has redemption, purpose, a point. This is metamodernism’s complicated relationship with story. There’s still a residual postmodern skepticism about all stories and storytelling, but also a growing recognition that we can’t live outside of stories and storytelling—at least in the subjective, “my story” sense. There’s still a residual postmodern skepticism about all stories and storytelling, but also a growing recognition that we can’t live outside of stories and storytelling. Perhaps it’s downstream from social media turning us all into performers for audiences, but it feels like there’s a pressure to “find your story” (a.k.a. your brand/niche), own it, and guard it from others who might want to manipulate or leverage it for their purposes. The 2026 comedy Power Ballad touches on some of these themes of creative ownership, as does Taylor Swift in her “Taylor’s Version” series of rerecorded albums. The recent movie Digger explores the way creative control and story-crafting can be PR—shaping one’s image or the reputation of someone you love. I Play Rocky is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told. As much as this sort of storytelling is pitched as empowerment and agency, however, it also feels burdensome and exhausting. Do we really find freedom when we’re constantly obsessing over our story, or our backstory (e.g. TikTok “lore drop” trend ), and how it’s perceived by online fans and followers? The story poverty in today’s world won’t find a satisfying resolution in hyperindividuated narrative obsession. What we really need is a grander story—something bigger than “my story,” bigger than your story. What’s truly freeing is not owning our own story but seeing ourselves as part of God’s story—owned by him, our lives not our own. This is our only hope in life and death .

title: How the Lord’s Supper Fuels Spiritual Growth
summary: Calvin shows us that the Lord’s Supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time.
summary_zh: 最近,我(和我的同龄人)经历了一些皈依天主教的教区人士. 我和这些皈依者交谈时, 他们发现在将面包和葡萄酒与耶稣的身体和血进行鉴别方面受到鼓励。 我听到过这样的话:乔治牧师,我喜欢耶稣在谈论主的晚餐,他说,“谁吃我的肉,谁喝我的血,谁在我体内,我就在他体内”(John 6:56)。 如果我每天把耶稣带到我的身体里, 虽然这种现象似乎更频繁地发生,
title_zh: 主的晚餐如何促进灵性成长
content: Recently, I (and my peers) have experienced a number of parishioners converting to Catholicism. As I’ve talked to these converts, they’ve consistently brought up the Lord’s Table. They find encouragement in identifying the bread and wine with Jesus’s body and blood. I’ve heard statements such as this: Pastor George, I like the idea that Jesus was talking about the Lord’s supper when he said, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). My faith just feels more real if I’m literally bringing Jesus into my body on a daily basis. While this phenomenon seems to be happening with greater frequency, it’s not totally new. Years ago, I served alongside a man at an ordination service for another pastor in our city. I hadn’t met this man before; I only knew he had until recently been a professor at a Reformed and evangelical seminary. This man preached a solid message on Jesus’s call for ministers of the gospel, and I thanked him for it. Then, the next day, I saw him being interviewed on TV. I tuned in just as he explained, I needed more realism than my tradition provided, so during lunch I would walk down to the local Roman Catholic parish and take the Eucharist. To unite literally with Jesus’s body and blood was more deeply satisfying to me than the “mystery of union with Christ” my church taught. So, I resigned my post at the seminary and went home to Rome. I could relate other conversations with those who have left the Reformed faith and joined the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, or Anglo-Catholic traditions. A similar theme runs through them all: the desire for a more transformational, sensory reality than what the Reformed view of the Lord’s supper provides. Is this critique valid? How would John Calvin respond to the critique that if you follow the Reformed view of the supper, you’re missing out on its power? Transformed at the Table Sometimes, in an effort to have biblically faithful theology, Reformed Christians speak only of what the communion elements are not . I’m painfully aware of my of shortcomings in this regard. This can inadvertently drive some believers to seek out a more “real” experience in other traditions. We can get caught up in debating the exact nature of the bread and wine and forget to ask the more pressing question: How should this meal change me today? Let’s look back at Calvin’s teachings on communion. When we do, we’ll recover a renewed vision for the table, one that sees it as a divine encounter that motivates a transformed life of profound gratitude and obedience. In short, Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In Calvin’s “ Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper ,” he writes that the supper fuels the believer’s spiritual growth in at least three ways. 1. The supper assures us of our inheritance in Christ. Calvin teaches that Jesus uses his table to assure us of our inheritance. He doesn’t merely mean that the supper gives us a psychological boost. He means that assurance comes by means of a real union between Christ and the believer, and he means that our experience of this union is expedited by faithfully partaking in the covenant meal. Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In his commentary on Ephesians, Calvin writes , “Paul says that we are members of his [Christ’s] flesh and of his bones. Do we wonder then, that in the Lord’s Supper he holds out his body to be enjoyed by us, and to nourish us unto eternal life?” Calvin insists that by faith, Christians are made members of Jesus’s fleshly human body, so at communion, we experience all the benefits of spiritual union with him. Christ took on flesh so that in his ascended state, he might be a channel of righteousness to the believer, pouring into him all that Christ’s human life accomplished. As a result of Jesus’s incarnation and death, God the Father established what Calvin calls a “holy brotherhood” between his Son and those united to his human flesh in salvation. What assurance! 2. The supper confirms and increases faith. Calvin sees the supper as a public and dramatic statement that God has atoned for the sins of the elect. God gives us this dramatic reenactment because he loves us. He knows “our faith is slight and feeble” and “unless it be propped up on all sides and sustained by every means, it trembles, wavers, totters, and at last gives way.” The Lord’s supper is a God-ordained means of “propping up” our faith, not because the supper is necessary to confirm God’s Word but because it improves our faith. In the supper, we experience a dramatic reenactment in which the ascended Christ, through his Holy Spirit, lifts our hearts to heaven. Christ does this for us, Calvin says, because regular communion with him strengthens us for the spiritual discouragements that inevitably come through besetting sin, temptation, and trials. Calvin views the sacraments as a means that cause Christ to “grow in us” so that our faith is fed more and more with Christ himself. Christians may experience any number of trials throughout their weeks that cause Christ’s spiritual, unseen realities to feel less plausible and real. Yes, our weak faith “trembles, wavers, and totters.” But when we come to the table, Christ gives us a public, dramatic reenactment that confirms his reality to our consciences and increases our faith. 3. The supper motivates and enables obedient Christian living. Calvin says, “There cannot be a spur which can pierce us more to the quick than when He makes us, so to speak, see with the eye, touch with the hand, and distinctly perceive the inestimable blessing of feeding on His own substance.” Thus, at the table, says Calvin, we’re compelled to a new obedience rooted in a grateful response to the blessings we receive there in Christ. Calvin’s conviction that the Lord’s supper provides occasion for this grateful celebration and response led him to structure worship services with this emphasis. In Calvin’s order of worship, the whole service is one long expression of gratitude in which the worshiper brings every aspect of his sin-sickness to the Savior. It concludes at the table where believers gratefully witness the Lord’s healing of all diseases dramatized. Calvin wouldn’t allow worshipers to enjoy this gratitude in private, because it’s a gift to share and a motivation that fuels outward and practical acts of “faith and charity” to others. This aspect of the supper that drives the worshiper closer to his brothers and sisters in Christ is the final distinctive of Calvin’s sacramental theology. Living Out Our Union with Christ As Christ, from love, pours out his life for the believer, the believer also pours out his life for others. So, each time you take the Lord’s supper by faith, you live out of your union with Christ, and he lives in and through you, making you new. Each time you take the Lord’s supper by faith, you live out of your union with Christ, and he lives in and through you, making you new. So, the next time you come to the Lord’s table, come expectantly. The living, risen Christ will use communion as fuel for your spiritual growth.
